26-050.r: Right to Information → a legal right under RTI Act 2005 and, per Supreme Court decisions, also a Fundamental Right; aims: empower citizens, transparency, accountability, curb corruption.

26-051.r: RTI Act 2005 Preamble mentions all four → transparency of information, revelation of information, informed citizenry, paramountcy of the democratic ideal.

26-052.r: RTI Act 2005 objectives → empower citizens, transparency and accountability of government, contain corruption, make democracy work for people; not 'empower women and weaker sections'.

26-053.r: RTI Act 2005, Section 6(2) → applicant need not give any reason or personal details for seeking information; the other options were provisions of the Act then.
26-053.c: No answer printed (*); the explanation shows option (b) is the one not provided in the Act.

26-054.r: RTI Act: Sections 18, 19, 25 → powers and functions of Central Information Commission; Section 12 is not. Raj Narain case (1976) → information right under Article 19.

26-055.r: RTI Act, Section 20 penalty → imposed by Central Information Commission or State Information Commission (not High Court).

26-056.r: Central Information Commission → constituted 12-10-2005 under RTI Act 2005; covers all Central Public Authorities; powers in Sections 18, 19, 20, 25.
26-056.h: CIC powers run 18-19-20, then jump to 25.

26-057.r: Information Commissioners' tenure → notified by Government of India after RTI (Amendment) Act, 2019; now 3 years or 65 years of age.
26-057.c: No answer printed (*): after the 2019 amendment none of the options (5 or 6 years) is the current tenure.

26-058.r: State Information Commissioners → appointed by Governor on recommendation of Chief Minister (Chair), Leader of Opposition in Assembly, a CM-nominated Cabinet Minister (Section 15(3)); no High Court Chief Justice.

26-059.r: State Information Commission → State Chief Information Commissioner + not more than ten Commissioners; eminent persons (law, science, journalism, etc.); cannot be a member of a Legislature.

26-060.r: Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan (MKSS), founded 1990 by Aruna Roy, Nikhil Dey, Shankar Singh → people's movement for the Right to Information (RTI Act).

26-061.r: Namit Sharma vs Union of India (2012) → case related to the Right to Information Act, 2005.
26-061.t: Lily Thomas and Nandini Sundar are not the RTI case; Namit Sharma is.

26-062.r: RTI Act 2005 → has raised sense of responsibility in bureaucracy, but still has miles to go; A and R both true, R not the explanation.

26-063.r: RTI Act 2005 objective → secure access to information under control of public authorities (Section 2); records, documents, works can be inspected and samples taken.

26-064.r: Madras High Court (division bench) → RTI applicant must disclose the object of seeking information; the RTI Act 2005 itself has no such requirement.

26-065.r: Citizen's Charter → nine basic elements (service standards, openness, consultation, access and choice, fairness, redress, etc.); 'inspection of agency's work' is not one.

26-066.r: Forest Rights Act, 2006 (Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers) → nodal agency for implementation: Ministry of Tribal Affairs (Section 12).
26-066.t: Not the Ministry of Environment, Forest & Climate Change, despite 'forest' in the Act's name.

26-067.r: Forest Rights Act, 2006, Section 6(1) → Gram Sabha initiates process to decide individual/community forest rights; then enquired at Tehsil and District levels.

26-068.r: National Green Tribunal Act, 2010 → based on right to a healthy environment under Article 21 (Right to Life); NGT established 18.10.2010.

26-070.r: Appeal against National Green Tribunal decision → to Supreme Court within ninety days; NGT set up 18.10.2010 under NGT Act 2010.

26-071.r: Land Acquisition Act, 1894 (British) → for acquiring land for public bodies and companies, not land reform; replaced by Right to Fair Compensation ... Act, 2013.

26-072.r: Code on Wages, 2019 replaced four laws → Payment of Wages Act 1936, Minimum Wages Act 1948, Payment of Bonus Act 1965, Equal Remuneration Act 1976; not Contract Labour Act.

26-073.r: Indian Contract Act → 1872 (not 1870); Companies Act → 2013; Partnership Act → 1932; Sale of Goods Act → 1930.

26-074.r: Prevention of Seditious Meetings Act → 1907 (not 1908); Explosive Substances Act, Indian Criminal Law Amendment Act, Newspaper (Incentive to Offence) Act → 1908.

26-075.r: Chronology: Lex Loci Act 1850 → Bengal Tenancy Act 1885 → Age of Consent Act 1891 → Indian University Act.
26-075.h: The correct order is simply I, II, III, IV.

26-076.r: Official Secrets Act, 1923: Section 6 → unauthorised wearing of police/military uniform; Section 7 → interfering with police/military officers (not Evidence Act); celebratory gunfire → Arms Act.

26-077.r: Disaster Management Act → passed 2005; President's assent 23 December 2005; 11 chapters, 79 sections.

26-079.r: National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA) → ex-officio Chairman: Prime Minister; set up under Disaster Management Act (23 December 2005); up to nine members; five-year term.

26-080.r: COVID-19 lockdown powers → Disaster Management Act, 2005 and Epidemic Diseases Act, 1897 (Section 2 invoked on 11 March 2020).
26-080.h: Lockdown used one old law (1897 epidemic) and one new law (2005 disaster).

26-081.r: Forest Conservation Act → enacted 1980; effective 25 October 1980.

26-082.r: Biological Diversity (Amendment) Act, 2023 → assent and Gazette publication on 3 August 2023; amends Biological Diversity Act, 2002; replaces imprisonment with civil penalties.

26-083.r: Community Reserve → declared by State Government (Section 36C, Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972), not Centre; managed under Section 36D, not by Chief Wildlife Warden; only two statements correct.

26-084.r: Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers' Rights Act → passed 2001; protects plant varieties and rights of farmers and plant breeders.

26-085.r: Aadhaar (SC verdict) → authentication data not kept beyond 6 months; private corporations barred from Aadhaar ecosystem; mandatory for Consolidated Fund benefits, not insurance products.

26-086.r: Aadhaar → 12-digit random number issued by UIDAI to residents of India; not proof of citizenship or domicile; can be deactivated or omitted.
26-086.t: Aadhaar is for residents, not only citizens, so it is no proof of citizenship.

26-087.r: IT Act, 2000 (e-governance): legal recognition of electronic records → Section 4; electronic signatures → Section 5; use in government → Section 6; electronic gazette → Section 8.

26-088.r: RTE Act, 2009: teacher qualifications set by academic authority authorised by Central Government (Section 23(1)), not State Council; primary teachers must pass Teacher Eligibility Test (NCTE guidelines).

26-089.r: Waqf (Amendment) Bill, 2024 (in Lok Sabha 8 August 2024) → transparency, governance and accountability of Waqf properties; reforms in registration, records, administration.

26-090.r: State Food Commission → established under Section 16 of National Food Security Act, 2013.

26-091.r: Consumer Protection Act, 1986 → consumers can take food samples for testing; legal heir can complain after consumer's death; a small fee is payable for complaints.

26-092.r: District Consumer Commission (Rules, 2021) → complaints up to 50 lakh rupees; State can set up more than one in a district; one member must be a woman (all true).

26-093.r: Consumer Protection Act, 1986 → District Forum in each district; hears claims up to twenty lakh rupees (not fifty); above twenty lakh → State Commission.

27-001.r: Supreme Court of India → inaugurated 28 January 1950.

27-002.r: Supreme Court → established by the Constitution of India; inaugurated 28 January 1950; succeeded the Federal Court (Government of India Act, 1935).

27-003.r: Appointment of Supreme Court and High Court Judges → based on Sapru Committee Report (1945) under Sir Tej Bahadur Sapru; set up by Non-Party Conference, November 1944.

27-004.r: Power to increase number of Supreme Court Judges → Parliament; Article 124 provides for formation of the Supreme Court.

27-005.r: Supreme Court → Part V, Chapter IV, Article 124; Articles 124 to 147 cover its composition and jurisdiction; in the 1950s it had a Chief Justice and seven Judges.
27-005.c: No answer printed (*): the sanctioned strength has changed since the paper, so the book marks none of the options.

27-006.r: Original Constitution (1950) → Supreme Court of a Chief Justice and 7 puisne Judges; Parliament may increase the number (Article 124).
27-006.c: No answer printed (*): the number of Judges has since been raised, so the book treats the question as outdated.

27-008.r: Supreme Court Judge (Article 124(3)) → citizen of India and High Court Judge for 5 years, or High Court advocate for 10 years, or distinguished jurist; appointed by President.
27-008.h: Advocates need double the time: 5 years as Judge, 10 as advocate.

27-010.r: Supreme Court Judge resigns by writing to the President; appointed by President by warrant under hand and seal; strength: CJI + up to thirty-three Judges (originally seven).

27-012.r: SC Judge removed (Article 124(4)) → President's order after address by each House (majority of total membership + two-thirds present and voting), for proved misbehaviour or incapacity.

27-013.r: Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968 → Speaker can reject a motion to remove an SC Judge; Constitution does not define 'incapacity and proved misbehaviour'; removal by President after Parliament's address.

27-015.r: Retirement age → Supreme Court Judges 65 years; High Court Judges 62 years.
27-015.h: Higher court, higher age: SC 65, HC 62.

27-017.r: Salaries of Supreme Court Judges → determined by Parliament by law (Article 125(1)); until then as in the Second Schedule.

27-018.r: Supreme Court autonomy → President must consult CJI on appointments; Judges' salaries charged on Consolidated Fund of India; removal by President with Parliament's special majority, not by CJI.
hi: Consolidated Fund of India (भारत की संचित निधि)

27-019.r: Parliament can enlarge Supreme Court's jurisdiction on Union List matters (Article 138); SC administrative expenses, incl. staff salaries and pensions, charged on Consolidated Fund of India; both statements false.

27-020.r: Retired Supreme Court Judge → cannot plead or act in any court or authority in India (Article 124(7)); bar on retired permanent High Court Judges → Article 220.

27-021.r: Acting Chief Justice of India → appointed by President (Article 126) when CJI post is vacant or CJI cannot act; no additional judges in Supreme Court.

27-023.r: Supreme Court Judges → appointed by President after consulting such SC and HC Judges as he deems necessary (Article 124(2)); CJI always consulted for other Judges.

27-024.r: Collegium System for appointing Judges → adopted by Supreme Court in 1993; origin in the Three Judges Cases.

27-025.r: Supreme Court Collegium → Chief Justice of India + 4 senior-most Judges.

27-026.r: SC Collegium → five members: CJI + four senior-most Judges; majority opinion prevails; not created by a law of Parliament.

27-027.r: NJAC (99th Amendment, 2014) → CJI (Chair), two senior SC Judges, Union Law Minister, two eminent persons (chosen by PM, CJI, Leader of Opposition); struck down in 2015.
hi: National Judicial Appointments Commission (राष्ट्रीय न्यायिक नियुक्ति आयोग)

27-028.r: Second Administrative Reforms Commission → recommended appointing higher court Judges with participation of Executive, Legislature and Chief Justice of India.

27-030.r: Ad hoc Judges in Supreme Court (Article 127(1)) → when quorum is lacking; CJI requests them with President's prior consent, after consulting the High Court's Chief Justice.

27-032.r: Article 128 → CJI, with President's prior consent, can ask a retired SC Judge (or qualified ex-HC Judge) to sit as SC Judge; High Courts too can review own judgments.

27-033.r: Cases involving interpretation of the Constitution → minimum 5 Supreme Court Judges (Constitution Bench).

27-034.r: Substantial question of law on interpreting the Constitution → minimum five SC Judges; benches kept odd (3, 5, 7, 9, 11) to avoid a tie.

27-035.r: Centre-State disputes → Supreme Court's original jurisdiction (Article 131), excluding other courts; covers disputes between Government of India and States, and among States.

27-039.r: Writs for Fundamental Rights → Supreme Court (Article 32) and High Courts (Article 226); so SC's writ power is not exclusive.
27-039.t: SC's original jurisdiction in inter-governmental disputes is exclusive; its writ power is not.

27-040.r: Supreme Court can hear appeals from Court Martial too (Armed Forces Tribunal Act, 2007); constituted 1950; highest court of appeal.

27-041.r: Court of Record (Article 129) → its judgments have evidentiary value and cannot be questioned in any court; can punish for its own contempt.

27-042.r: Courts of Record → Supreme Court (Article 129) and High Courts (Article 215); both can punish for contempt of themselves.

27-043.r: Court of Record → Article 129 (not 124, which establishes SC); Article 143 → advisory; 132 → appellate; 136 → special leave to appeal.
27-043.t: Article 124 creates the Supreme Court; Court of Record status is Article 129.

27-044.r: Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 → on H.N. Sanyal Committee (1961) report; SC and HCs punish contempt (Articles 129, 215); Constitution does not define civil/criminal contempt.

27-045.r: M.L. Sachdev vs Union of India → wilful non-compliance with court order treated as contempt; civil contempt = wilful disobedience (Section 2(b), Contempt of Courts Act, 1971).

27-046.r: Supreme Court sits in Delhi or other places the CJI appoints with approval of the President (Article 130).
27-046.t: Needs the President's approval, not Parliament's or a majority of Judges.

27-047.r: Basic Structure doctrine → Kesavananda Bharati vs State of Kerala (1973), thirteen-Judge bench, 7:6; Parliament cannot damage basic structure under Article 368.

27-049.r: Articles 32, 226, 227 → inviolable basic structure (judicial review by SC and High Courts, Kesavananda Bharati); Article 245 not.

27-050.r: Basic Structure Theory → source: judicial interpretation (Kesavananda Bharati case), approved in Minerva Mills case, 1980; limits amending power under Article 368.

27-051.r: Largest SC bench → 13 Judges, Kesavananda Bharati (1973); second largest → 11 Judges, Golaknath vs State of Punjab (1967).

27-052.r: Golaknath vs State of Punjab → 'Fundamental Rights enable a man to chalk out his life in the manner he likes best'.
